title: MME
body:
The `Content-Type` header, telling the receiver **what kind of bytes these are**. Spelled MIME
(*Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions*) outside the course notes; Evan's file server calls
it MME and means the same thing.

```
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Type: image/png
```

It exists because [[HTTP]] bodies are just bytes and nothing about them says whether they are
a page, an image, or data. The browser decides what to do purely from this header: render it,
display it, download it, or hand it to `response.json()`.

A general file server therefore has to map file extensions to types itself, which is the
`mimeTypes` table in [[Node.js]]'s file-server example:

```js
const mime = mimeTypes.find(m => m[0] == path.parse(filename).ext);
resp.writeHead(200, {"Content-Type": mime[1]});
```

[[Express]] does this for you, which is a large part of why nobody writes that loop twice.

Getting it wrong is not cosmetic: serve JSON as `text/plain` and `fetch(...).then(r =>
r.json())` still works, but serve HTML as `text/plain` and the browser shows you the tags. The
header also has to match on the way *in*, which is how a server knows whether a POST body is
form data or [[JSON]]. See [[HTTP]] and [[Fetch]].
